option_a.notes: The screenshots independently support the review: the center town uses a much wider aerial scale than the close-up district dioramas; terrain and infrastructure do not continue across their boundaries; feathered rectangular and oval edges remain perceptible; several districts appear to float; and mobile cropping exposes large empty regions without creating a convincing sense of adjacent geography. A genuinely continuous illustration would solve these problems most completely and could make panning feel like exploration rather than moving a collage. However, compositing the existing assets more carefully would not be sufficient: scale, camera angle, lighting, depth, and topology would all need reconciliation. A single coherent map also becomes increasingly expensive and fragile as locations are added. Literal adjacency may suggest geographical relationships between professions that are incidental rather than meaningful to the game's premise.

option_b.notes: This direction accepts the strongest visual fact already present: each district is a self-contained miniature. Consistent mounts, normalized footprints, deliberate spacing, and an unmistakable connecting path would convert apparent compositing failures into a readable world-selection grammar. It preserves the illustrations and suits the game's collection of realistically different workplaces without claiming they occupy one literal landscape. It should improve tapping and mobile composition because nodes can be arranged around viewports rather than geographic realism. Its limitation is scale: fifty detailed islands on one pannable surface would become crowded, slow to navigate, and difficult to remember unless divided into regions or pages. The center town must receive the same categorical treatment as every other node; otherwise the present scale hierarchy will continue to feel accidental.

option_c.name: Hierarchical Atlas with Focused District Views
option_c.notes: Use a visually unified, intentionally simplified overview as the navigation layer, with each location represented by a consistent marker, thumbnail, or cropped landmark. Selecting one opens a focused district view where its existing rich illustration and mini-games can occupy the screen at an appropriate scale. The overview supplies relational continuity without pretending that independently authored scenes share one camera or physical scale. This directly solves the mobile screenshots' clipping, ambiguous off-screen content, tiny targets, and large low-information areas: broad navigation happens at overview scale, while detailed exploration happens in a bounded scene. It also supports fifty locations through regions, categories, or atlas pages without enlarging one endless canvas. Existing artwork remains useful, though producing standardized overview representations and transition framing entails some new design work. Compared with B, it sacrifices the immediacy of seeing every full diorama simultaneously but avoids turning future growth into an increasingly unwieldy constellation.

recommendation_reasoning: C offers the strongest structural fit for both the current asset reality and the product's likely growth. The present screen is not merely under-polished: it combines incompatible representational scales on one spatial plane, so CSS-level blending cannot make it read as one geography. A would deliver the richest continuous world but carries disproportionate art cost and makes every future addition a map-wide composition problem. B is the best low-cost near-term architecture and would be a substantial improvement, but a single constellation becomes less usable as the location count approaches fifty. C separates overview navigation from detailed place exploration, allowing each profession-rich scene to retain its character while establishing a coherent and scalable interaction model, especially on mobile.
requires_human_product_decision: Whether the map should communicate literal geography or a conceptual journey among professions and places.
Whether entering a district through a second navigation level is acceptable or immediate one-tap access to mini-games is required.
Whether the product roadmap genuinely anticipates approximately fifty locations, since that materially favors a hierarchical architecture.
Whether standardized overview markers or thumbnails may be derived from existing artwork without commissioning replacement district illustrations.
Whether region grouping should reflect geography, profession families, learning progression, or another taxonomy.
